title: Culvert Nine
passages:
The dot on the movement trace kept walking, ahead of the cart, steady as a meter tick. Kass gripped the cart handles and looked up the grade. The rails ran dark into the cut, no headlight, no plate, just the shape of a ghost train eating the ore line toward them.

"Ghost," Kass said. "Plate stripped. It won't answer hails."

Ospina shifted the seal die in their pocket. "It won't stop for bodies on the rail either."

"We're not asking it to stop for bodies," Kass said. "We're asking it to check for a flag."

The old flag was a length of relay orange tied to a broken surveyor's pole. Kass planted it in the sleeper ties, stepped onto the rail with Ospina, and waved it hard. The cart's wheels squeaked against the steel. Far up the grade, the train's air brakes hissed once—a soft check, like it noticed, like it cared—and then the hiss stopped. The rig did not slow. It did not stop. Ghost trains drove themselves between nodes; they had no crew to see a flag, no brake handle for a person to pull.

"Into the cut," Kass said.

They hauled the cart off the rail and dragged it into the drainage cut beside the grade, metal scraping on rock. The train screamed past, a wall of dark steel and displaced air that shoved the cart sideways and left the rail humming. Kass stayed flat until the rumble faded into the dark. Their ears were ringing. The cart had tipped onto one wheel, its load of empty crates rattling.

Then the dot from the movement trace stepped onto the road.

It was a person, wrapped in a Culvert Nine coat, carrying a hand lamp and a clipboard. They stopped ten paces away and looked at the empty cart.

"Two of you," the lookout said. Their voice was dry, sharp enough to cut grease. "Cart's empty. You came down-line for cargo and brought nothing back."

"We were waiting for a train that doesn't stop for people," Kass said. "Who are you?"

"Lookout. Brill's crew. I count the heads that walk my road." The lookout tapped the clipboard. "You're Kass. Dispatcher, post 71. Ospina. Seal authority, bay four. You're down from Anza with a red plate and no resupply."

Ospina's hand stayed on their pocket. "Brill's crew. You hoard the skim."

"We eat it," the lookout said. "Brill's people have been drawing rations off the totalizer all night while Anza starves. Every seal you're missing went through this station. Every calorie."

The totalizer was the station meter that counted stock out of the storeroom by receiving mark. If Brill's crew had been drawing against it, the food wasn't lost—it was earmarked, already eaten by someone else's winter.

"Where is Brill?" Kass asked.

"Back room. With the man who made the seals hot." The lookout stepped aside, lamp swinging. "You want the scrubbers? You want Anza eating past dawn? You talk to Voss. And you bring something to trade. Brill doesn't take promises. She takes stock."

The lookout turned and walked back toward the pump station, leaving Kass and Ospina with the empty cart and the dark grade. Somewhere ahead, the ghost train had vanished down the ore line, plate-less and unlogged, while Culvert Nine ate Anza's eleven seals one ration at a time.

The pump house sat at the bottom of a dry sump, its door hung crooked on one hinge, and they went in past a turbine the size of a rail car that hadn't turned since the water left the Interior. Inside it smelled like dust, cold oil, and bread.

Then the lamp found the crates.

They were stacked the length of the pump hall, pallet on pallet, every one of them ringed in chalk: *Br-4*. Cornmeal in fifty-pound sacks. Fuse wire on wooden spools, enough to rewire a relay shop twice. Canned milk three tiers deep with the labels sun-bleached to the color of weak tea. And on the low pallet by the sump grate, six cases with an Anza relay shop routing tag still wired to the handles—scrubber cartridges, the kind that pull carbon back out of a breath so a man doesn't have to work for every lungful he takes.

Kass crouched at the low pallet and counted the cases out loud. Twice. As if the number might improve.

"Four restarts," Ospina said. "Rhea's got four restarts and a hand pump."

"Then she'd better keep pumping," a woman said from the stair.

She came down slow, a short woman in a receiver's coat with the cuffs cut off, a hand lamp in one fist and nothing in the other. Behind her the lookout set the clipboard on a nail and stayed by the door.

"Brill," Kass said.

"You walked my road and read my chalk. I'm not going to pretend to be somebody else." Brill put her lamp on a crate lid so it lit all of them at once. "That's Anza's winter on my floor. Cornmeal, milk, fuse wire. I know exactly whose it is. I've known since the second run came in."

"Then hand it over," Ospina said.

"No."

Ospina's jaw worked. "You've got our food, our wire, and eleven seals' worth of Anza's roster, and you're going to stand there and tell me no."

"I'm going to stand here and tell you the rule, and then you can be as angry as you like about it." Brill didn't raise her voice. "Nothing leaves this hall without a trade. Not a sack. Not a cartridge."

Saul spoke from the door, tapping the clipboard. "The totalizer's a brass wheel behind glass. Every case that crosses that chalk line, I strike the receiving mark on the tally and the wheel turns. No power in this station and it still counts. That's the whole point of it." They shrugged. "Nine people eat off that wheel. Two of them are mine."

"Nine," Kass said. "You've got nine people and a pump station's worth of Anza's resupply."

"I've got nine people and a road that gets walked by things with no plate on them, dispatcher. Don't talk to me about hoarding."

"I'm not talking about hoarding. I'm talking about a man at Anza relay shop breathing on a rubber disc and a hand pump, on a node with a red plate and a frozen line."

"Everybody's got a man," Brill said. "I had a storeroom once, at a real station with a real line behind it. A man with a clean voice and a full clipboard took four crates off my floor and left me a promise written on line paper. I ate the paper. It was terrible." She picked her lamp back up. "I trust a full storeroom over any person's word, and I've earned that. My people eat through winter off this pile, or they don't eat. That's not cruelty, that's arithmetic."

"Arithmetic," Ospina said. "You've got four crates of arithmetic sitting there that were routed to a relay shop."

"Then buy them."

Kass stood up. "With what? You've seen our plate. We came down-line with an empty cart because a ghost train doesn't stop for people, and you counted us at the door."

"I don't take promises," Brill said. "I take stock, and I take trades. Bring me something I can stack."

Behind her, deeper in the station, something hissed. Then a clunk. Then, patient as a pump that still had water in it, the hiss and the clunk again.

Saul didn't look up from the tally. "That's been going since midnight."

"That's the man who made your seals hot," Brill said. "He's the only one under this roof with a trade you can afford."

"There's a man at Anza relay shop with four restarts and a disc of glove rubber for a diaphragm," Kass said. "Six cases, Brill. Cartridges. You've got Ivo's next year stacked by the sump grate and you're calling it arithmetic."

"I'm calling it stock," Brill said. "Buy it or walk back up my road."

"Maybe we can buy it," Ospina said.

Kass turned. "With what?"

Ospina pulled the glove off their right hand and held it up. On the thumb was a brass ring, worn smooth, a number stamped inside the band. "Seal authority. Bay 4, Shift 2. Live as of this morning." They crouched at the cornmeal pallet and found the seal puck wired through the sack stitching, a lead crimp with a reader window in it. "Every crate carries two halves. Sender reseals it at the bay, receiver counters it where it lands. Two clean halves and it's freight. One half and it's a derelict, and derelicts are what men like Pell haul off as ballast." They looked up. "Red plate freezes resupply. It doesn't freeze trade. Trade needs two halves. I've got one of them on my hand."

"Until Kettering's desk opens at 08:00 and decides you don't," Kass said, already pulling the handset off their belt. "Anza board, this is Kass, down-line. Teodoro. Say it slow, I've got wind in the set."

"Talk," Teodoro said. "I've got one hand on a bulb and the other on a man's shoulder, so make it worth the squeeze."

Ospina pressed their thumb into the reader window and held it there while the puck counted. The window went amber. Then it went a flat, patient red.

Teodoro read it out twice, slower the second time. Sender: Bay 4, Shift 2, resealed 05:52. Counter: absent. Receiving ring accepted as live, authority flagged. "It took you," he said. "It took you as the receiver. It wants the counter half off Bay 4 to close the sender, and there isn't one, because nobody at Bay 4 ever sent this. Ospina, you just put a clean ring on stolen goods with no counter behind it."

"Can you strike it?" Ospina said.

"Not from here. Only the counter strikes a counter, or the desk does, at eight." A pause, the sound of a bulb compressing. "Congratulations. You've got a dirty mark on a flagged authority four hours before your own review. When that desk opens, you'll walk in with nothing on your hand and everything on your record."

"So I'd better be right the first time," Ospina said, and pulled the glove back on.

Kass crouched by the puck. "Four restarts, and the fourth is the last one that catches. After that Rhea's pumping a dead man's chest for the look of the thing."

Ospina's other hand went to their coat pocket, thumbed it open, and stayed there over something small and hard, without drawing it out. They didn't press it. They looked at the six cases by the sump grate the way a person looks at a number they can't make add up, and they took their hand off the pocket empty.

Saul hadn't moved from the door. "Wheel hasn't turned," they said. "Nobody's crossed the chalk. That ring cost you and it didn't buy you a sack."

Brill picked her lamp up off the crate lid.

"You stamped my floor," she said. "Under my rule that's not a trade, that's a mess, and I've had enough of your mess for one night." She walked past the milk tiers toward the back of the hall, where the hiss and clunk kept its patient time. "But I'm not the one who writes the halves. Come on. Take it up with the man who made it hot."

Kass and Ospina followed her between the pallets, past the sump grate, to a door with light under it and a curtain of seal dust hanging off the frame. Brill put her hand flat on the wood.

"Mind the dust," she said. "It gets in everything."

Behind the door, the hissing stopped mid-stroke. In the new quiet, somebody set a brass die down on a bench with the care of a man who had all night.

Brill pushed the door and the warmth came out first, oil-warm and close, a room built for one man and one machine.

The machine sat on a steel bench: a reseal rig, a squat press with a puck cradle and a hand lever, the kind a bay uses to crimp a fresh sender half over a torn one so freight reads clean at the next node. Beside it lay the receiving die, a brass counter-stamp heavy enough to break a thumb, its face cut with the Bay 4 mark. Pucks in a coffee can. A kettle on a hot plate, actually steaming. A cot in the corner with the blanket folded square.

The man at the bench was maybe fifty, gray at the temples, sleeves rolled, hands clean. He set the die down with the care of somebody who had all night, and turned on the stool without standing.

"You brought me the Anza crew," he said. "All of them but the one everybody wants."

"Calder Voss," Kass said.

"Badge 2209." He said it the way a man says his own shoe size. "Don't bother looking at the board. I took myself off it at Kettering this morning, and it's the cleanest thing I ever did. No alarm, no scrub line. A forger who forges himself out is just weather."

"You know why we're here," Ospina said.

"I know why everybody's here tonight. There's a man at Anza who can put a face to me, and an officer who wants the two of us in a drawer by first light." Voss lifted the kettle, poured, didn't drink. "You're Marlowe's people. He gave you my name over the set, I heard it. Good for him. Better memory than the pod had."

"You're not worried," Kass said.

"Worry's a thing you spend when you've got options." He nodded at Ospina's gloved hand. "You stamped her floor. Red on amber. A clean receiving ring with no counter behind it, because there was never a Bay 4 sender. Because I'm the one who resealed those crates at 05:52, and I don't stay to counter my own work."

"So counter it," Ospina said. "You've got the die."

"And put my thumb on a puck with your live seal already in it? That makes me the far end of a chain a line-trust officer is building with his whole chest." Voss almost smiled. "No. But I can make all eleven clean. Every case on that floor. Cornmeal, milk, the six boxes of scrubbers by the grate, all of it legal enough the board takes it and the desk can't call it stolen."

Kass didn't move. "How."

"By paying for it." Voss turned the brass die a quarter-turn so the mark faced up. "Here's what nobody down this line understands about erasing yourself. It isn't free, and it isn't forever. I bought one morning off the board. I bought being weather." He tapped the die. "Cleaning those seals costs me the exact thing I un-listed myself to keep. The whole reason I'm nobody right now. You want Anza eating past dawn, and the price of it is the one thing I did all this to not pay."

"Say it plain," Ospina said.

"No." For the first time the calm had an edge under it. "Not till you tell me what you're actually offering, because it isn't stock and it isn't a promise, Brill's made that clear." He looked past them, through the door, to the six cases by the sump grate. "You came down here for cargo. I'm the only one under this roof who can make it move. So sit, or don't, and tell me what a node with a red plate figures it's got that's worth more to me than my one clean morning."

Voss set the kettle back on the hot plate without pouring a second cup.

"Here's the chain," he said. "Nobody down your line reads a seal the way the desk reads it. The desk doesn't ask who really sent the cornmeal. It asks whose name sits on the sender half and whose thumb sits on the counter, and whether those two close. Right now your ring's live and there's no sender to meet it. That's your red."

Ospina nodded once. They knew the shape of it.

"So I reseal the eleven," Voss said. "Fresh sender halves, crimped clean over the torn ones. My die, my thumb, my name. Badge 2209, Calder Voss, resealing authority, Bay 4 Shift 2. The second that name hits the board as the far end of your chain, the counters close, Ospina's ring goes from red to clean, and every case on Brill's floor reads legal at the next node. The board can't call it stolen. The desk can't. Anza eats."

"Then do it," Ospina said.

"You're not listening." The edge came back under the calm. "I un-listed myself this morning to be nobody. A name that signs for eleven reseals is the opposite of nobody. The moment 2209 is back on that board as the counter, every flag I shed reattaches. Fraud, reseal, the pod, all of it, in this room, on me, before the pucks finish cooling. You don't just clean the food. You hang me to do it."

Kass got there first. "You'd go down with the seals."

"I'd *be* the seals," Voss said. "That's the trade your red plate can't argue with. Your winter walks out legal because a flagged man walked into the light to sign for it."

Silence, except the hot plate ticking.

"So the thing that makes you nobody," Ospina said slowly, "is the thing that keeps Ivo from breathing."

"Now you're reading it." Voss almost looked pleased. "Your receiver can't stand in for my counter. Ospina's ring is clean and flagged and worth nothing without a Bay 4 sender crimped behind it, and I'm the only Bay 4 sender still breathing who can pull the lever. So here's Brill's arithmetic, done honest: my name for your food. You put me on the board, I go down, you eat. Clean halves, closed chain."

Brill had gone still by the door. Saul's pencil stopped on the tally.

"That's not fair," Kass said. "That's you selling us your own arrest and calling it freight."

"It's the only stock I've got you can stack," Voss said. "Everything else on that floor is Brill's, and she doesn't take promises."

Ospina's hand went to their coat pocket again, thumbed it, and left it there. The chipped die was inside, the one they'd found in the tool void and never stamped with. It could cut a Bay 4 mark. It couldn't sign for one. A forger's die with no forger's name behind it was just one more thing on this line with no counter.

"There's no clean version of this," Kass said. "We came to carry the food home, and there's no home for it that doesn't cost somebody the board."

"Somebody," Voss agreed. "Doesn't have to be me."

Kass looked up. "You've got another way to close the chain. Something that isn't your name."

"I've got a price," Voss said. "Not a name. A price. And it isn't stacked on Brill's floor and it isn't in your pocket." He picked the die back up, careful, a man with all the night left in the world, and set it square in the cradle of the press. "But you don't get to hear it standing in my doorway with an empty cart. Sit down, Anza. You're carrying the one thing I want, and it's the reason every soul under this roof is still awake."
